newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajikistan may legalise opposition groups.
newsitem.headline: Tajikistan may legalise opposition groups.

text.p: A senior Tajik official said on Tuesday the former Soviet republic, torn apart by four years of civil war, was considering legalising opposition parties and organisations.
"We are going to look at the legalisation of opposition parties and political organisations at the talks," Talbak Nazarov, Tajikistan's foreign minister, told Reuters.
He spoke just before leaving for the Iranian capital Tehran where he will represent the government at a further round of peace negotiations with the country's armed Islamic opposition.
The main protagonists in the civil war agreed to a ceasefire last December during talks in neighbouring Afghanistan. A military deal was agreed last month in Moscow.
Nazarov will meet opposition representative Akbar Torajonzoda in Tehran, with talks centering on a political settlement expected to last around 10 days.
"Organisations at the moment are mostly military-political," Nazarov said in reference to the remote, mountainous republic's kaleidescopic array of warlords and regional fiefdoms.
"They must disarm and become purely political organisations," Nazarov said.

The talk of political liberalisation marks the first real, if tentative, step away from war in Tajikistan. Just four months ago when the latest in a series of ceasefires was established, few expected it would last more than a few days -- but it did hold.
Then in February, the government and the opposition hailed a preliminary power-sharing agreement, giving each side an equal number of seats on a 26-member National Commission for Reconciliation.

The commission was limited to members of government and Islamic opposition. Diplomats fear the commission could sideline other groups not given seats, although legalisation of opposition political parties would give them a greater voice.
However, some opposition leaders have expressed concern over the eventual process of legalisation.
Dzhumaboy Niyazov, leader of the outlawed Democratic Party, said: "The government insists on disarming before legalisation but we think it should be the other way round."
A Western diplomat based in Dushanbe also warned of problems. "A big obstacle to the signing of a political protocol is the legalisation of the Islamic Renaissance Party," he said.
The party is the main organisation standing behind the Islamic opposition.
"Even some Tajik officials have said they doubt an accord on this will be reached at the talks in Tehran," he said.
